pages.title: 🧭 00 — Learning Map & Decision Framework
pages.objective: Choose a SQL technique from the required population and output grain.
pages.body: ## خريطة بصرية السؤال الأول مش اسم الدالة. السؤال: الصف الواحد في النتيجة يمثل إيه؟ ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["What should one output row represent?"] --> C["More columns from a related table"] Q --> E["Do related rows exist?"] Q --> G["One row per group"] Q --> W["Keep every detail row and add a value"] Q --> S["Stack compatible rows"] Q --> N["Name the steps"] C --> JOIN["JOIN"] E --> EX["EXISTS"] G --> GB["GROUP BY"] W --> WIN["Window function"] S --> SET["UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT"] N --> CTE["CTE"] ``` شكل النتيجة واحد من دول: قيمة واحدة، صفوف كتيرة، صف لكل مجموعة، أو نفس الصفوف مع قيمة تحليلية. > صفحة البداية السريعة للمكتبة: كيف أختار تقنية SQL المناسبة، وكيف أراجع الاستعلام قبل أن أثق في نتيجته. # 1. SQL Problem-Solving Workflow ```txt Business Question ↓ Define Population ↓ Define Grain ↓ Identify required tables / relationships ↓ JOIN / Filter ↓ Transform: CASE / Subquery / CTE ↓ Aggregate or Window ↓ Validate result shape ↓ Validate edge cases + NULLs ↓ Check execution plan when needed ``` # 2. Choose the Technique | Need | Usually start with | | --- | --- | | Categorize rows | CASE | | Filter by a scalar/list produced by another query | Subquery in WHERE | | Build an intermediate table-like result | Derived Table / CTE | | Check whether related rows exist | EXISTS | | Row-by-row dependency on the outer query | Correlated Subquery | | Keep detail rows while adding an aggregate | Window Function | | Combine attributes from related tables | JOIN | | Multi-stage, readable transformation | CTE | # 3. The Grain Check Before writing SQL, finish this sentence: > One output row represents . Then verify that every JOIN and aggregation preserves or intentionally changes that grain. # 4. The Population Check Ask: - What rows enter the calculation? - Which rows are excluded before CASE/AVG/SUM? - What becomes NULL? - What exactly is the denominator? This is especially important for percentages and conditional aggregation. # 5. Result-Shape Checklist ```txt Scalar → one value Rowset → many rows Grouped result → one row per group Window result → original rows + analytic value Derived table / CTE → named intermediate rowset ``` # 6. Common Logic Traps - ELSE 0 can corrupt averages and percentages when non-target rows should be excluded. - COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(expression) ignores NULL expressions. - AVG() of raw rows is not the same as average of already aggregated groups. - A JOIN can multiply rows and silently inflate aggregates. - A correlated subquery may be logically correct but expensive; inspect the execution plan when scale matters. # 7. Final Review Questions 1. Is the business definition unambiguous? 2. Is the grain explicit? 3. Is the population correct? 4. Are NULL semantics intentional? 5. Is the denominator correct? 6. Could a JOIN multiply rows? 7. Would a CTE or window function make the intent clearer? 8. Have I tested edge cases? 9. Does the result reconcile to an independent calculation?

pages.title: 🧱 01 — SQL Foundations — Complete Reference
pages.objective: Distinguish logical query meaning, physical execution, filtering and grouping.
pages.body: ## خريطة بصرية ده ترتيب المعنى، مش ترتيب تنفيذ المحرك. Window functions تتحسب بعد التجميع، فمش بتتفلتر جوه WHERE. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["1 FROM / JOIN"] --> B["2 WHERE"] --> C["3 GROUP BY"] --> D["4 HAVING"] --> E["5 SELECT"] --> F["6 DISTINCT"] --> G["7 ORDER BY"] --> H["8 LIMIT"] ``` ## Purpose The canonical foundation for understanding SQL as a relational query language. This page owns the mental models that every later module depends on. ## 1. The SQL Mental Model SQL is declarative: you describe the result you want, while the database optimizer decides how to execute it. The most important distinction is between: - Logical query meaning — what rows/columns the query should return. - Physical execution — how the engine actually obtains that result. A strong SQL analyst reasons about both, especially when correctness and performance matter. ## 2. Tables, Rows, Columns, and Grain A table is a relation containing rows and attributes. Before writing a query, identify the grain: what one row represents. Examples: - orders: one row per order. - order_items: one row per order line. - student_term_snapshot: one row per student × term × active program. ### Why grain matters Many SQL bugs are not syntax bugs. They are grain mistakes that silently multiply rows or produce incorrect aggregates. Before JOIN, GROUP BY, or a window function, ask: > What does one input row represent, and what should one output row represent? ## 3. Logical Query Processing Order A useful conceptual order is: FROM / JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT/OFFSET Window functions are evaluated after the grouped result exists, which is why they can use aggregate results but generally cannot be used directly in WHERE. This order explains common patterns such as filtering a window-function result in an outer query or CTE. ## 4. SELECT Is Not "Just Choosing Columns" SELECT can: - project columns, - compute expressions, - evaluate scalar functions, - perform conditional logic, - calculate aggregates, - define window calculations. Example: ```sql SELECT product_id, quantity * unit_price AS revenue FROM order_items; ``` ## 5. WHERE vs HAVING WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. ```sql SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spend FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'Completed' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000; ``` Interview trap: HAVING is not simply a "second WHERE". The two operate at different stages and grains. ## 6. NULL and Three-Valued Logic NULL means missing/unknown/not applicable; it is not the same as zero or an empty string. Comparisons involving NULL do not evaluate to ordinary TRUE/FALSE. SQL uses TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN. Correct checks: ```sql WHERE phone IS NULL WHERE phone IS NOT NULL ``` Incorrect: ```sql WHERE phone = NULL ``` Key functions/patterns: - COALESCE() for fallback values. - NULLIF() for converting a value to NULL conditionally. - COUNT(*) counts rows. - COUNT(column) ignores NULL values. ## 7. DISTINCT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the selected projection. Do not confuse: - removing duplicate output rows, - identifying duplicate business entities, - fixing row multiplication caused by an incorrect join. Using DISTINCT to hide a bad join is a correctness smell. ## 7.5 Keys (PK / FK / Candidate / Composite) - Primary key: uniquely identifies a row. - Foreign key: references a key in another table. - Candidate key: any minimal column set that could serve as a unique identifier. - Composite key: uniqueness requires multiple columns together. Understanding keys is a prerequisite for reasoning about JOIN cardinality (see Module 05). ## 7.6 Filtering Principles Prefer explicit, intention-revealing predicates: - range: amount >= 100 AND amount < 500 - membership: status IN ('Paid', 'Shipped') - pattern: name LIKE 'Am%' - null: discount IS NULL For timestamp ranges, prefer half-open intervals when appropriate: >= start AND < end. ## 8. Expressions, Aliases, and Reuse Column aliases improve readability, but alias visibility depends on SQL dialect and logical query stage. A select-list alias normally cannot be referenced by another expression in the same select list as though it were an already-materialized column. Prefer a CTE/derived table when a calculated result becomes an input to later logic. ## 9. Data Type Thinking SQL expressions are type-sensitive. Understand: - integer vs decimal/numeric, - text vs numeric, - date vs timestamp, - explicit casting, - implicit conversion rules, - integer division risks. Example: ```sql SELECT CAST(total_amount AS numeric) / NULLIF(order_count, 0) FROM ...; ``` ## 10. Determinism and Ordering A result set is not guaranteed to have a meaningful order unless ORDER BY is specified. Likewise, operations such as ROW_NUMBER() require an ordering definition if deterministic ranking is expected. Avoid assuming physical table order, insertion order, or clustered storage order is a logical ordering guarantee. ## 11. Core Safety Checks Before Aggregation Before writing a KPI query: 1. Define the population. 2. Define the grain. 3. Define the measure. 4. Define exclusions. 5. Check for NULLs. 6. Check join cardinality. 7. Validate row counts before and after joins. 8. Reconcile a sample against source records. ## 12. Common Anti-Patterns ### SELECT * Useful for exploration, risky in reusable production logic. ### DISTINCT as a band-aid May conceal duplicate-producing joins. ### Filtering after aggregation when row filtering was intended Can produce inefficient or semantically wrong queries. ### Comparing to NULL with = Produces no matches because NULL = NULL is not TRUE. ### Assuming row order Without ORDER BY, order is not guaranteed. ## 13. Mini Real-World Case Suppose management asks: > "What is the average completed-order value per customer in 2026?" A robust approach is: - establish the population: completed orders in 2026, - establish grain: one order per row before customer-level aggregation, - aggregate at customer grain, - calculate the desired metric at the correct level. The main lesson is that business definitions must precede SQL syntax. ## 14. Interview Traps Q: Why can WHERE not normally contain an aggregate like SUM(amount) > 1000? Because WHERE filters rows before grouping/aggregation. Use HAVING for group-level aggregate filters. Q: Why can a LEFT JOIN unexpectedly behave like an inner join? A predicate on the right-side table placed in WHERE can eliminate the NULL-extended rows created by the left join. Move the predicate into the ON condition when preserving unmatched left rows is required. Q: Why does COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(column)? COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values of that column. ## Ownership Rule This page owns foundational SQL reasoning. Other notes may reference these concepts, but should not duplicate the full canonical explanation.

pages.title: 🧩 02 — Database, Schema & Data Modeling — Complete Reference
pages.objective: Inspect keys, relationships, constraints and missing values before querying.
pages.body: > جزء من سلسلة Intermediate SQL: هذا المرجع مخصص لفهم بنية الـdatabase قبل أي تحليل — استكشاف الجداول، الـPK/FK والعلاقات، الـconstraints، وأساسيات التعامل مع NULL. # 1. سير عمل الاستكشاف الواقعي (The Real-World EDA Workflow) عندما تدخل Database جديدة في شغل حقيقي، لا تبدأ مباشرة بـ SELECT * على كل شيء. فكّر بالترتيب: ```txt Database ↓ 1. Discover tables & relationships ↓ 2. Inspect schema / ERD ↓ 3. Identify PKs & FKs ↓ 4. Understand data types & constraints ↓ 5. Sample rows ↓ 6. Check NULLs / missing / suspicious codes ↓ 7. Summarize distributions ↓ 8. Explore relationships between variables ↓ 9. Build intermediate datasets when useful ↓ 10. Answer the business question ``` ## مثال واقعي: Student Analytics Database تخيل أنك انضممت لفريق BI في جامعة، وعندك tables مثل students، enrollments، courses، departments. قبل أن تسأل "ما متوسط الـ GPA؟" لازم تعرف: ما هو الـgrain لكل table؟ ما هو الـprimary key؟ ما هي الـforeign keys؟ هل GPA يمكن أن يكون NULL؟ هل 0 GPA حقيقي أم missing code؟ > Core principle: فهم الـ semantics والـ schema يسبق التحليل. # 2. استكشاف محتوى الـDatabase ## 2.1 Database Client الـ database client هو البرنامج الذي تتصل من خلاله بالـ database وتنفذ SQL وتفحص الـ schema. يساعدك في اكتشاف Table names، Column names، Data types، Constraints، Relationships. > في الشغل الحقيقي، ارجع أيضًا إلى الـ ERD والـ data dictionary والـ database documentation؛ لا تعتمد على SQL وحده لفهم business meaning. ## 2.2 Sampling Rows ```sql SELECT customer_id, country, signup_date FROM customers LIMIT 10; ``` ### مهم الـ rows ليست مرتبة افتراضيًا. إذا كنت تريد ترتيبًا محددًا: ```sql SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY signup_date DESC LIMIT 10; ``` > LIMIT يقلل عدد الصفوف المعروضة؛ لا يعني بالضرورة أن database قرأت فقط هذه الصفوف منطقياً في كل execution plan. # 3. أساسيات NULL NULL تعني unknown / missing value، وليست رقمًا ولا string فارغًا. ## 3.1 Correct NULL syntax ❌ خطأ: WHERE salary = NULL — ✅ صحيح: WHERE salary IS NULL وللبحث عن القيم الموجودة: WHERE salary IS NOT NULL ## 3.2 COUNT(\*) vs COUNT(column) COUNT(*) يعد عدد الصفوف. بينما COUNT(salary) يعد عدد القيم غير NULL فقط. إذن: ```txt Missing salary = COUNT(*) - COUNT(salary) ``` ### مثال واقعي: Data quality check ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows, COUNT(student_id) AS student_id_present, COUNT(gpa) AS gpa_present, COUNT(*) - COUNT(gpa) AS missing_gpa FROM students; ``` ## 3.3 COUNT(DISTINCT column) COUNT(DISTINCT country) يعد عدد القيم المختلفة غير NULL. لكن SELECT DISTINCT country FROM students; يمكن أن يظهر NULL كواحد من القيم المميزة. > Exam / interview trap: DISTINCT قد يعرض NULL، بينما COUNT(DISTINCT column) لا يعد NULL. # 4. المفاتيح والعلاقات (Keys & Relationships) ## 4.1 Primary Key (PK) الـ Primary Key هو العمود/مجموعة الأعمدة التي uniquely identify كل row. خصائصه: Unique، Not NULL، يحدد هوية الصف. ## 4.2 Foreign Key (FK) الـ Foreign Key هو column يشير إلى key في table أخرى، وغالبًا إلى primary key. ```txt students --------- id (PK) ↑ │ FK │ enrollments ------------ student_id (FK) ``` الـ FK يساعد على فرض referential integrity: القيمة الموجودة في الـ child table يجب أن تتوافق مع قيمة مسموحة في الـ referenced table، أو تكون NULL إذا كان العمود يسمح بذلك. ## 4.3 Self-reference ```txt employees --------- id PK manager_id FK → employees.id ``` يسمح بتمثيل hierarchy (CEO ← Manager ← Employees). ## 4.4 الـFK ليس شرطًا لعمل JOIN ```sql SELECT * FROM company c JOIN fortune500 f ON c.ticker = f.ticker; ``` إذا لم توجد FK بين الجدولين، فهذا لا يمنع الـ JOIN. الفرق أن database لا تفرض نفس referential constraint على ticker. > Key distinction: JOIN هو query operation؛ FOREIGN KEY هو database constraint. # 5. قيود الأعمدة (Column Constraints) الـ constraints تحدد ما القيم المسموح بها. ### UNIQUE كل قيمة غير NULL يجب أن تكون مختلفة: email TEXT UNIQUE ### NOT NULL العمود لا يقبل NULL: student_id INT NOT NULL ### CHECK يفرض business/data rule: CHECK (gpa >= 0 AND gpa <= 4) أو CHECK (end_date >= start_date) ### PK / FK PK يحدد row uniquely، FK يربط row بـ referenced row ويحافظ على referential integrity. > Important: Constraints are not the same as data types. Data type يحدد طبيعة القيم التي يمكن تخزينها؛ constraint يضيف قواعد إضافية على تلك القيم. # 6. أخطاء المقابلات والامتحانات - COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column): الأولى تعد الصفوف، الثانية تتجاهل NULL. - COUNT(DISTINCT column): يعد القيم المختلفة غير NULL فقط. - SELECT DISTINCT column: ممكن يرجع NULL كقيمة مميزة. - column = NULL: خطأ؛ استخدم IS NULL / IS NOT NULL. - FK vs JOIN: الـFK هو constraint؛ الـJOIN هو query operation. تقدر تعمل JOIN من غير FK. # 7. Cheat Sheet ```sql -- Sample SELECT * FROM table_name LIMIT 10; -- Missing SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(column_name) AS missing FROM table_name; -- Distinct values SELECT DISTINCT column_name FROM table_name; -- Distinct count SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) FROM table_name; ``` --- ### 🔗 مراجع ذات صلة

Important: Constraints are not the same as data types. Data type يحدد طبيعة القيم التي يمكن تخزينها؛ constraint يضيف قواعد إضافية على تلك القيم.

pages.title: 03 — Data Types, Casting & NULL Logic — Complete Reference
pages.objective: Reason about data types, casting and three-valued NULL logic.
pages.body: ## Purpose Canonical home for SQL data types, casting/conversion, NULL semantics, three-valued logic, and safe handling of missing/invalid values. ## 1. Data Type Mental Model A data type describes what values mean and what operations are valid. Choose types by business meaning, not by how the value happens to look. Common families: - Numeric: integer, decimal/numeric, floating point - Character: char, varchar, text - Temporal: date, time, timestamp, interval - Boolean - Dialect-specific types such as arrays, JSON, UUID ## 2. Exact vs Approximate Numbers Use numeric/decimal for values where exactness matters, especially financial amounts. Floating-point types are approximate and can introduce representation differences. ## 3. Casting Explicit casting makes transformations intentional: ```sql CAST(amount_text AS numeric) ``` PostgreSQL also supports: ```sql amount_text::numeric ``` Be careful: a cast can fail when source values are malformed. ## 4. NULL Is Not a Value NULL represents unknown, unavailable, or missing information. It is different from: - 0 - '' - FALSE Do not use = NULL or <> NULL.8 ```sql WHERE manager_id IS NULL ``` ## 5. Three-Valued Logic SQL predicates can evaluate to TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. For example, 10 = NULL is UNKNOWN. A WHERE clause retains only TRUE rows. This explains many subtle filtering and anti-join bugs. ## 6. NULL Functions ### COALESCE Returns the first non-NULL expression. ```sql COALESCE(discount, 0) ``` ### NULLIF Returns NULL when two expressions are equal. ```sql NULLIF(quantity, 0) ``` Useful for preventing division by zero: ```sql revenue / NULLIF(quantity, 0) ``` ## 7. NULL in Aggregates COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX generally ignore NULL inputs, with result behavior depending on whether usable values exist. Always distinguish no rows, all NULL, and zero as business states. ## 8. NULL in JOINs NULL = NULL is not TRUE. Therefore rows with NULL join keys do not match using ordinary equality. When NULL-safe matching is required, use a dialect-appropriate approach intentionally. ## 9. NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS NOT IN can produce surprising results when its subquery contains NULL. For relational existence logic, NOT EXISTS is often safer and clearer. ## 10. Data Quality Pattern For raw data, separate: 1. invalid values; 2. missing values; 3. legitimate zero/empty values; 4. unknown/unavailable values. Do not blindly replace every NULL with zero. ## 11. Real-World BI Example A student dataset may contain NULL graduation dates for active students. Replacing them with an arbitrary date would corrupt cohort and completion analysis. Preserve NULL when it represents “not yet applicable.” ## 12. Common Traps - = NULL instead of IS NULL - COUNT(column) interpreted as row count - replacing NULL with zero without business meaning - NOT IN with nullable subqueries - integer division assumptions - silent/unsafe implicit casts - using floating point for exact financial calculations ## 13. Ownership This page is the canonical deep reference for Data Types, Casting, NULL, and three-valued logic. Other SQL notes should link here instead of reproducing the full theory. pages.title: 04 — Filtering & Conditional Logic — Complete Reference
pages.objective: Define row populations and conditional classifications with explicit precedence.
pages.body: ## Purpose Canonical home for row filtering, predicates, CASE expressions, conditional expressions, and the reasoning behind WHERE/HAVING/filter placement. ## 1. WHERE as Population Control WHERE defines which source rows enter the next logical stage of the query. ```sql SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'Completed'; ``` Think of filtering as defining the analytical population. ## 2. Core Predicate Families - comparison: =, <>, >, >=, <, <= - range: BETWEEN - membership: IN - pattern: LIKE - NULL: IS NULL, IS NOT NULL - existence: EXISTS ## 3. AND / OR / NOT Use parentheses whenever business logic could be ambiguous. ```sql WHERE country = 'EG' AND (status = 'Active' OR status = 'Pending') ``` Do not rely on readers remembering operator precedence. ## 4. CASE CASE maps conditions to values. ```sql CASE WHEN amount >= 10000 THEN 'High Value' WHEN amount >= 5000 THEN 'Medium Value' ELSE 'Low Value' END ``` Use it for classification, conditional calculations, flags, and controlled business rules. ## 5. Simple vs Searched CASE Simple CASE compares one expression against values. ```sql CASE status WHEN 'A' THEN 'Active' WHEN 'I' THEN 'Inactive' END ``` Searched CASE evaluates independent conditions and is more flexible. ## 6. CASE in Aggregation A major analytical pattern: ```sql SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) ``` This is the bridge between conditional logic and KPI generation. ## 7. CASE and NULL Be explicit about NULL behavior. An unmatched CASE expression reaches ELSE, or returns NULL if no ELSE is supplied. ## 8. WHERE vs HAVING Use WHERE to reduce rows before grouping. Use HAVING to filter groups based on aggregate results. ## 9. Filter Placement with JOINs With LEFT JOIN, putting a right-table condition in WHERE can remove NULL-extended rows. Put the condition in ON when the intent is to preserve unmatched left rows. ## 10. Real-World Example Customer segmentation: - High value: lifetime revenue >= 50,000 - At risk: no completed order in 90 days - New: first order within 30 days Each classification should have an explicit population and precedence rule. ## 11. Interview Traps - WHERE vs HAVING - CASE without ELSE - overlapping CASE conditions - incorrect AND/OR precedence - filtering the right side of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE - confusing CASE with COALESCE ## 12. Ownership This page owns filtering and conditional logic. Deep subquery/CTE mechanics belong to Module 07; aggregation mechanics belong to Module 06.

pages.title: 🔗 05 — JOINs & Relationship Reasoning — Complete Reference
pages.objective: Predict JOIN cardinality and prevent duplicated measures.
pages.body: ## خريطة بصرية لو العميل عنده أوردران مبالغهم 100 و 50، ودفعتان مبلغهم 80 و 70، الـ JOIN الخام يعمل 4 صفوف. مجموع مبلغ الأوردر على الصفوف دي يبقى 300 مش 150. ```mermaid flowchart TD R["What is the relationship?"] --> M["Many side joined to another many side"] R --> OK["Many side joined to one parent row"] M --> Fan["2 orders x 2 payments = 4 rows"] Fan --> Wrong["SUM of the order amount becomes 300"] M --> Fix["Aggregate each child table to the parent grain first"] Fix --> Right["Then join the summaries: orders 150, payments 150"] OK --> Check["Still compare row count before and after the join"] ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD L["LEFT JOIN"] --> On["Right-table filter in ON"] L --> Wh["Right-table filter in WHERE"] On --> Keep["Unmatched left rows stay"] Wh --> Lose["Unmatched left rows disappear"] ``` ## Purpose The canonical reference for JOINs, relationship semantics, cardinality, row multiplication, and join correctness. ## 1. The Core Mental Model A JOIN combines rows from two row sets according to a matching condition. The most important question is not "which JOIN syntax should I use?" but: > What relationship exists between the two row sets, and what output grain do I need? ## 2. Cardinality Typical relationship patterns: - 1:1 — one row on each side matches one row. - 1:M — one parent row matches many child rows. - M:1 — many child rows map to one parent. - M:M — many rows can match many rows. A JOIN can increase row count. That is not automatically wrong; it is a consequence of the relationship. ## 3. INNER JOIN Returns only matched rows. ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id; ``` Use when unmatched rows are irrelevant or intentionally excluded. ## 4. LEFT JOIN Returns every row from the left side, with matching right-side data where available. ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id; ``` Use for questions such as: > Which customers have no orders? ```sql WHERE o.order_id IS NULL ``` ## 5. RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN RIGHT JOIN preserves the right side; it is often rewritten as a LEFT JOIN by swapping table positions for readability. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides and is useful for reconciliation/matching problems. ## 6. CROSS JOIN Produces the Cartesian product of two row sets. If A has 100 rows and B has 20 rows, a pure Cartesian product has 2,000 rows. Use intentionally for scenarios such as generating combinations, calendars, scenarios, or cohort × metric matrices. Accidental cross joins are a serious correctness/performance problem. ## 7. Join Conditions A robust join condition should express the true business relationship. Example composite relationship: ```sql ON a.student_id = b.student_id AND a.term_code = b.term_code ``` Joining on only one component can create false matches. ## 8. One-to-Many Aggregation Trap Suppose customers has one row per customer and orders has many rows per customer. This is valid: ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id; ``` But joining orders to another one-to-many table such as payments may multiply rows. Example: - customer has 3 orders, - customer has 2 payments, - joining both raw child tables by customer can create up to 6 combinations. This is the classic fan-out / row multiplication problem. ## 9. The Safe Aggregation Pattern Aggregate each many-side independently before joining when the business grain requires it. ```sql WITH order_totals AS ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(order_amount) AS total_orders FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ), payment_totals AS ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(payment_amount) AS total_payments FROM payments GROUP BY customer_id ) SELECT c.customer_id, COALESCE(o.total_orders, 0) AS total_orders, COALESCE(p.total_payments, 0) AS total_payments FROM customers c LEFT JOIN order_totals o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id LEFT JOIN payment_totals p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id; ``` ## 10. JOIN vs EXISTS Use a JOIN when you need columns from the related table or need to combine row sets. Use EXISTS when the question is primarily: > Does at least one related row exist? ```sql SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id ); ``` This avoids creating duplicate customer rows merely to test existence. ## 11. LEFT JOIN + WHERE Trap This: ```sql FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'Completed' ``` can remove customers with no matching orders. When preserving all customers is required, consider: ```sql FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'Completed' ``` ## 11.5 JOIN vs IN IN expresses membership in a set. EXISTS expresses existence of a related row and is often safer for correlated relational logic. Be careful with NULL semantics when comparing NOT IN against NOT EXISTS — NOT IN against a set containing NULL can silently return zero rows. ## 12. Joining on Nullable Columns Ordinary equality does not match NULL to NULL. If business semantics require treating two missing values as a match, use an explicit dialect-appropriate null-safe comparison strategy and document it. ## 13. Self JOIN A table can be joined to itself. Example employee-manager hierarchy: ```sql SELECT e.employee_name, m.employee_name AS manager_name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id; ``` ## 14. Bridge Tables and Many-to-Many Relationships A many-to-many relationship is often represented through a bridge/junction table. Example: students ↔ student_courses ↔ courses Never assume a direct many-to-many join preserves a unique row grain. ## 15. Join Validation Checklist After a new JOIN, compare: - row count before vs after, - distinct business keys before vs after, - unmatched rows, - duplicate keys on either side, - expected cardinality, - aggregates before vs after. A strong analyst treats join validation as part of query development, not a final cleanup step. ## 16. Real BI / DWH Case In a warehouse, joining a fact table to dimensions is normally many-to-one from fact to dimension. If a supposedly unique dimension key matches multiple dimension rows, the fact can multiply and KPIs can be overstated. Therefore, referential integrity and dimension uniqueness are analytical correctness controls, not just database administration concerns. ## 17. Interview Traps Q: Why did my total revenue double after adding a JOIN? Likely row multiplication caused by a one-to-many or many-to-many relationship. Inspect the grain and cardinality instead of adding DISTINCT blindly. Q: JOIN or EXISTS for "customers who placed at least one order"? EXISTS is often the clearer expression because the requirement is existence, not returning order columns. Q: Can LEFT JOIN increase rows? Yes. LEFT describes preservation of left rows; it does not guarantee one output row per left row. ## Ownership Rule This page owns JOIN semantics, cardinality, row multiplication, and join correctness. Other modules may use examples but should link back here for deep reasoning. CASE Statements — Complete Reference

pages.title: 📊 06 — Aggregation & Grouping — Complete Reference
pages.objective: Choose the grouping grain and define a correct KPI denominator.
pages.body: ## خريطة بصرية WHERE يشيل صفوف. GROUP BY يغيّر الـ grain لصف واحد لكل مجموعة. HAVING يشيل مجموعات. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Input rows"] --> B["WHERE"] --> C["GROUP BY"] --> D["HAVING"] --> E["One row per group"] ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["Do you still need the detail rows?"] --> No["No"] Q --> Yes["Yes"] No --> GB["GROUP BY"] Yes --> Win["Window function"] GB --> Note["An average of averages is wrong when the groups have different sizes"] ``` ## Purpose The canonical reference for GROUP BY, aggregate functions, grain transitions, conditional aggregation, and KPI-safe aggregation. ## 1. Aggregation Is a Grain Transformation The deepest way to understand aggregation is: > GROUP BY transforms many input rows into one output row per group key. Example: - Input grain: one row per order. - GROUP BY customer_id. - Output grain: one row per customer. Every selected expression must therefore be compatible with the new group grain. ## 2. Core Aggregate Functions Common aggregates: - COUNT - SUM - AVG - MIN - MAX - dialect-specific statistical/percentile functions Example: ```sql SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(amount) AS revenue, AVG(amount) AS avg_order_value FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id; ``` ## 3. COUNT(\*) vs COUNT(column) COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. This distinction matters whenever a column can be missing. ## 4. SUM and NULL SUM(column) ignores NULL inputs, but a group containing only NULL values may produce a NULL result rather than zero depending on dialect behavior. Use explicit business semantics: ```sql COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) ``` when zero is the correct interpretation. ## 5. AVG Is Not Always the Average You Think An average of averages can be wrong when subgroup sizes differ. Incorrect idea: ```txt (average of group A + average of group B) / 2 ``` Correct overall average requires weighting by the number of observations or aggregating the underlying numerator/denominator correctly. ## 6. GROUP BY and Selected Columns A selected non-aggregated column generally must be part of the grouping set or otherwise be functionally determined in a dialect-supported way. Conceptually: > Every output row must have an unambiguous value for every selected expression. ## 7. WHERE vs HAVING Use WHERE to remove input rows before grouping. Use HAVING to filter resulting groups. ```sql SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'Completed' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) >= 10000; ``` ## 8. Conditional Aggregation One of the most useful SQL patterns for BI/analytics. ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_orders, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders FROM orders; ``` For amounts: ```sql SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) ``` This pattern turns row-level conditions into multiple KPIs in one grouped query. ## 8.5 COUNT vs SUM(CASE) For counts of conditions, these two forms can express the same business idea: ```sql COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 END) ``` ```sql SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ``` But NULL behavior and readability should be considered when choosing between them. ## 9. DISTINCT Aggregation COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) answers a different question from COUNT(*). Example: > Number of unique customers who placed an order. ```sql SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders; ``` Do not confuse row count with entity count. ## 10. GROUP BY Multiple Dimensions ```sql SELECT college_code, term_code, COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) AS students FROM enrollment GROUP BY college_code, term_code; ``` Output grain becomes: one row per college × term. This explicit grain statement is extremely useful for validating BI datasets. ## 11. Aggregation After JOIN Always reason about whether the JOIN has changed the grain before aggregation. Dangerous: ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id; ``` If multiple payments exist per customer, order rows may multiply. Safer pattern: aggregate each many-side to the required grain before joining. ## 12. Semi-Additive Measures Not every metric can be summed across every dimension. Examples: - transaction revenue is usually additive across transactions/time, - account balance may be additive across accounts but not across time, - inventory balance often should use an end-of-period or snapshot logic rather than summing daily balances. Correct KPI design requires knowing the measure's additivity properties. ## 13. Grouping Sets, ROLLUP, and CUBE Advanced grouping features can generate multiple aggregation levels in one query. Concepts: - ROLLUP — hierarchical subtotals. - CUBE — combinations of grouping dimensions. - GROUPING SETS — explicitly requested grouping levels. Example: ```sql SELECT region, product_category, SUM(revenue) FROM sales GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, product_category); ``` These are especially useful for reporting and multidimensional summaries. ## 14. Aggregation vs Window Functions GROUP BY reduces rows. Window functions calculate across related rows while preserving the detail rows. Example: ```sql -- Aggregation: one row per customer SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id; ``` versus: ```sql -- Window: keeps one row per order SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total FROM orders; ``` This distinction is one of the most important interview concepts in analytical SQL. ## 15. KPI Design Pattern Before writing a KPI, define: Numerator → what counts toward the metric? Denominator → what is the comparison population? Grain → what is one observation? Population filters → which rows are eligible? Null treatment → missing, zero, excluded, or unknown? Join effects → can relationships multiply rows? Example conversion rate: ```txt successful_orders / eligible_orders ``` Do not calculate a ratio until both numerator and denominator populations are explicitly defined. ## 16. Real BI Case — Enrollment Suppose management asks for: > Active students by college and academic term. Input grain may be one student × term × program. If the business KPI is one student counted once per college × term, using COUNT(*) could overcount students enrolled in multiple programs. The correct metric may require: ```sql COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) ``` The business grain determines the SQL. ## 17. Validation Techniques For a new aggregate: - compare total rows to source expectations, - compare COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT business_key), - reconcile totals to a trusted report, - inspect a small sample manually, - test edge cases involving NULLs and duplicate keys. ## 18. Interview Traps Q: Why is COUNT(*) sometimes wrong for "customers"? Because rows may represent transactions, not customers. Use the count that matches the business entity, often COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id). Q: Why did SUM(revenue) increase after a JOIN? Usually because the JOIN multiplied fact rows before aggregation. Q: GROUP BY or window function? Use GROUP BY when you need fewer rows at a new grain. Use a window function when you need an analytical calculation while preserving row detail. ## 17.5 Common Analytical Mistakes (Checklist) - counting rows instead of entities; - averaging already-aggregated averages; - summing duplicated facts after a JOIN; - filtering with HAVING when WHERE could reduce data earlier; - forgetting NULL behavior; - mixing columns from incompatible grains; - grouping by too many columns and unintentionally producing a lower-level grain. ## Ownership Rule This page owns aggregation semantics, grouping, KPI-safe aggregation, grain transitions, and conditional aggregation.

flowchart LR

The canonical reference for GROUP BY, aggregate functions, grain transitions, conditional aggregation, and KPI-safe aggregation.
The deepest way to understand aggregation is:
GROUP BY transforms many input rows into one output row per group key.

items: Input grain: one row per order.
Output grain: one row per customer.

blocks.text: Every selected expression must therefore be compatible with the new group grain.

SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue,
       AVG(amount) AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
This distinction matters whenever a column can be missing.
SUM(column) ignores NULL inputs, but a group containing only NULL values may produce a NULL result rather than zero depending on dialect behavior.
when zero is the correct interpretation.
5. AVG Is Not Always the Average You Think
An average of averages can be wrong when subgroup sizes differ.
(average of group A + average of group B) / 2
Correct overall average requires weighting by the number of observations or aggregating the underlying numerator/denominator correctly.
A selected non-aggregated column generally must be part of the grouping set or otherwise be functionally determined in a dialect-supported way.
Every output row must have an unambiguous value for every selected expression.
Use WHERE to remove input rows before grouping.

SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'Completed'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 10000;
One of the most useful SQL patterns for BI/analytics.

SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders
FROM orders;
SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
This pattern turns row-level conditions into multiple KPIs in one grouped query.
For counts of conditions, these two forms can express the same business idea:
SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
But NULL behavior and readability should be considered when choosing between them.
COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) answers a different question from COUNT(*).
Number of unique customers who placed an order.
Do not confuse row count with entity count.

SELECT college_code,
       term_code,
       COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) AS students
FROM enrollment
GROUP BY college_code, term_code;
This explicit grain statement is extremely useful for validating BI datasets.
Always reason about whether the JOIN has changed the grain before aggregation.

SELECT c.customer_id, SUM(o.amount)
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id;
If multiple payments exist per customer, order rows may multiply.
Safer pattern: aggregate each many-side to the required grain before joining.
Not every metric can be summed across every dimension.

items: transaction revenue is usually additive across transactions/time,
account balance may be additive across accounts but not across time,
inventory balance often should use an end-of-period or snapshot logic rather than summing daily balances.

blocks.text: Correct KPI design requires knowing the measure's additivity properties.
Advanced grouping features can generate multiple aggregation levels in one query.
These are especially useful for reporting and multidimensional summaries.
Window functions calculate across related rows while preserving the detail rows.

-- Aggregation: one row per customer
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount)
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- Window: keeps one row per order
SELECT order_id,
       customer_id,
       amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total
FROM orders;
This distinction is one of the most important interview concepts in analytical SQL.
Null treatment → missing, zero, excluded, or unknown?
Do not calculate a ratio until both numerator and denominator populations are explicitly defined.
Active students by college and academic term.
Input grain may be one student × term × program.
If the business KPI is one student counted once per college × term, using COUNT(*) could overcount students enrolled in multiple programs. The correct metric may require:
The business grain determines the SQL.

items: compare total rows to source expectations,
reconcile totals to a trusted report,
test edge cases involving NULLs and duplicate keys.

blocks.text: Because rows may represent transactions, not customers. Use the count that matches the business entity, often COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id).

Usually because the JOIN multiplied fact rows before aggregation.
Use GROUP BY when you need fewer rows at a new grain. Use a window function when you need an analytical calculation while preserving row detail.

pages.title: 07 — Subqueries & CTEs — Complete Reference
pages.objective: Choose subqueries, EXISTS and CTEs from result shape and dependency.
pages.body: ## خريطة بصرية شكل الاستعلام الداخلي هو اللي يحدد الأداة، مش مكانه في الجملة. ```mermaid flowchart TD S["What does the inner query return?"] --> Scalar["One value"] S --> List["Many values, one column"] S --> Rel["Rows and columns"] S --> Row["It depends on the current outer row"] Scalar --> A["Scalar subquery"] List --> B["IN"] Rel --> C["Derived table or CTE"] Row --> D["Correlated subquery"] D --> E["Use EXISTS when the question is only existence"] ``` CTE بتسمي الخطوة. مش جدول مؤقت، ومش أسرع تلقائي. ## Purpose Canonical home for SQL subqueries and Common Table Expressions (CTEs), with emphasis on grain, scope, correlation, execution behavior, readability, and choosing the right pattern. ## 1. Core Mental Model A subquery is a query nested inside another query. The important question is not merely where it appears, but what shape it returns and how the outer query consumes it. Think in four shapes: - Scalar → one value - Single-column list → many values from one column - Derived table → rows and columns used as a relation - Correlated subquery → evaluated logically in relation to the current outer row ## 2. Subquery in WHERE Use when the business question is about membership or existence. ```sql SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN ( SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01' ); ``` ### IN vs EXISTS - IN expresses membership in a returned set. - EXISTS expresses whether at least one matching row exists. - For anti-matching, prefer NOT EXISTS when NULL behavior could make NOT IN unsafe. ## 3. Scalar Subquery in SELECT A scalar subquery returns one value per outer row. ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, (SELECT MAX(o.order_date) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS last_order_date FROM customers c; ``` Use it when the relationship is naturally one value per outer row. If the logic becomes complex or expensive, consider a JOIN or pre-aggregation. ## 4. Derived Tables A subquery in FROM becomes a temporary relational result for the outer query. ```sql SELECT customer_id, total_sales FROM ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ) s WHERE total_sales > 100000; ``` This is especially useful when you must aggregate first, then filter or join. ## 5. Correlated Subqueries A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query. ```sql SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.amount > 10000 ); ``` The key idea is row-relative logic: the inner condition depends on the current outer row. ## 6. Nested Subqueries A nested subquery contains another subquery. Nesting is valid, but deep nesting can hide business intent. Prefer a CTE or staged transformation when each logical step deserves a name. ## 7. CTEs A CTE names an intermediate query using WITH. ```sql WITH customer_sales AS ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ) SELECT * FROM customer_sales WHERE total_sales > 100000; ``` CTEs improve readability, decomposition, reuse within a statement, and debugging. They are primarily a query-organization mechanism; do not assume a CTE automatically materializes or improves performance in every database. ## 8. Multiple CTEs Use sequential CTEs when the analytical problem has clear stages. ```sql WITH monthly_sales AS ( SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, customer_id, SUM(amount) AS sales FROM orders GROUP BY 1, 2 ), ranked AS ( SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY sales DESC) AS rnk FROM monthly_sales ) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 10; ``` ## 9. Subquery vs CTE vs JOIN vs Window Function | Technique | Best fit | | --- | --- | | JOIN | Bring related attributes/rows together | | EXISTS | Test whether a related row exists | | IN | Membership in a set | | Scalar subquery | One value per outer row | | Derived table | Transform rows before outer query | | CTE | Name and stage complex logic | | Window function | Compare a row with related rows without collapsing grain | ## 10. Grain Is the Deciding Factor Before writing the query, state the grain. Example: - Source grain: one row per order line. - Required result: one row per customer. If you aggregate inside a subquery/CTE before joining to customers, you can control row multiplication and preserve the intended grain. ## 11. Real BI Use Case — Student Analytics Business question: Which students are currently active and have completed more credits than the average active student? ```sql WITH active_students AS ( SELECT student_id, earned_hours FROM enrollment_snapshot WHERE status_code = 'ACTIVE' ), avg_hours AS ( SELECT AVG(earned_hours) AS avg_earned_hours FROM active_students ) SELECT s.student_id, s.earned_hours FROM active_students s CROSS JOIN avg_hours a WHERE s.earned_hours > a.avg_earned_hours; ``` The CTE separates population definition from benchmark calculation, making the logic easier to validate. ## 12. Correctness Checks Before trusting a subquery/CTE solution: 1. What is the outer-query grain? 2. What shape does the inner query return? 3. Can the inner query return multiple rows where a scalar is expected? 4. Can NULL change the result of IN / NOT IN? 5. Will a JOIN be clearer or safer? 6. Does the transformation accidentally multiply rows? 7. Can each stage be validated independently? ## 13. Performance Notes - Reduce rows early when appropriate. - Pre-aggregate before joining when the target grain is higher than the source grain. - Use execution plans rather than assuming a CTE/subquery is faster. - Correlated logic can be elegant but should be measured on large datasets. - Index/filter columns that participate in selective predicates and joins where appropriate. ## 14. Interview Traps - A CTE is not automatically a temporary table. - A CTE is not automatically faster than an equivalent subquery. - EXISTS checks existence; it does not need to return the matching values. - A scalar subquery must logically produce at most one value for each outer row. - NOT IN can behave unexpectedly when the subquery contains NULL. - DISTINCT should not be used as a blind fix for row multiplication. ## 15. Canonical Ownership This page is the single canonical reference for Subqueries and CTEs. Legacy pages should preserve useful examples and applied material, but should point back here for the complete conceptual treatment. pages.title: 08 — Set Operations — Complete Reference
pages.objective: Combine compatible rows while controlling duplicates and set difference.
pages.body: ## خريطة بصرية Current = 1, 2, 3. Archived = 3, 4. UNION ALL يسيب الـ 3 مرتين. INTERSECT يرجّع 3 فقط. EXCEPT يرجّع 1 و 2. ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["What are you combining?"] --> Col["Columns from a related table"] Q --> Rows["Compatible rows from two results"] Col --> Join["JOIN"] Rows --> All["UNION ALL: keep duplicates"] Rows --> U["UNION: drop duplicate rows"] Rows --> I["INTERSECT: rows in both"] Rows --> X["EXCEPT: rows in the first result only"] ``` ## Purpose Canonical reference for combining result sets with UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT. ## 1. Set Operations vs JOINs JOIN combines columns across related rows. Set operations combine rows from compatible result sets. This distinction is fundamental. ## 2. UNION vs UNION ALL UNION combines result sets and removes duplicate rows. UNION ALL combines them without deduplication and is usually preferable when duplicates are meaningful or impossible by design. ```sql SELECT customer_id FROM current_customers UNION ALL SELECT customer_id FROM archived_customers; ``` ## 3. Column Compatibility Corresponding SELECT statements must have compatible numbers and types of columns. Column names are taken from the first query in the set operation. ## 4. INTERSECT Returns rows present in both result sets. Useful for finding overlap between populations. ## 5. EXCEPT Returns rows present in the first result set but absent from the second. Useful for gap analysis and reconciliation. ## 6. Real-World BI Use Cases - current vs archived customer populations - students enrolled in both programs - reconciliation between source and warehouse IDs - identifying records present in source A but missing from source B ## 7. UNION vs JOIN Decision Ask: - Need more columns from related records? → JOIN. - Need to stack compatible rows? → UNION/UNION ALL. - Need overlap? → INTERSECT. - Need difference? → EXCEPT / anti-join pattern. ## 8. Common Traps - using UNION when UNION ALL is intended - mismatched column meaning despite compatible data types - assuming UNION preserves duplicates - confusing set difference with a LEFT JOIN anti-join ## 9. Ownership This page is the canonical deep reference for SQL set operations.

pages.body: ## خريطة بصرية القوس على day 3 و day 4 و day 5. الصف الحالي هو day 5، والإطار ياخد صفّين قبله. ```mermaid flowchart TD P["PARTITION BY: who is in the same group"] --> O["ORDER BY: their sequence"] O --> F["FRAME: which of those rows enter this row's calculation"] F --> FN["FUNCTION: what to calculate"] ``` GROUP BY يختزل الصفوف. الـ window تسيب الصفوف وتضيف قيمة. # 🎯 الهدف من الدليل مرجع شامل للمذاكرة السريعة والعميقة لـ SQL Window Functions: المفهوم، الصياغة، ORDER BY، PARTITION BY، Fetching، Ranking، Paging، Window Frames، الحالات الخاصة، والأخطاء الشائعة. > الفكرة الذهبية: Window Function تحسب نتيجة اعتمادًا على مجموعة من الصفوف المرتبطة بالـ current row، مع إبقاء الصفوف الأصلية موجودة. الموضوع اتقسم لـ 8 صفحات فرعية حسب الفرع، عشان يبقى سهل تفتح اللي محتاجه بس وقت المذاكرة أو المراجعة السريعة، بدل ما تفتح صفحة واحدة ضخمة. --- ## 📂 الفهرس 1️⃣ الأساسيات: Window Functions, OVER, PARTITION BY, ORDER BY المفهوم الأساسي، الفرق مع GROUP BY، الشكل العام للـ OVER()، وترتيب ORDER BY جوه وبره OVER. 2️⃣ Ranking Functions: ROW\_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE\_RANK, NTILE مقارنة الثلاث دوال الترقيم، Tie-breaking، وNTILE للـ paging والـ bucketing (quartiles/deciles). 3️⃣ Fetching Functions: LAG, LEAD, FIRST\_VALUE, LAST\_VALUE الصف السابق/التالي، أول/آخر قيمة، وأهم فخ في LAST\_VALUE مع الـ default frame. 4️⃣ Aggregate Functions & Window Frames: Running/Moving Totals SUM/AVG/MAX كـ window functions، Window Frames بالتفصيل، ROWS vs RANGE، والـ Moving Average/Total. 5️⃣ أمثلة تطبيقية مركّبة (CTE + Patterns) CTE مع window functions، وأشهر الأنماط الجاهزة زي "Top 3 per group". 6️⃣ Paging & Pivoting تقسيم النتائج لصفحات بـ ROW\_NUMBER، وتحويل الـ Rows لـ Columns (Pivot / CROSSTAB). 7️⃣ GROUP BY Extensions: ROLLUP, CUBE, COALESCE, STRING\_AGG Subtotals والـ Grand Total، الفرق بين ROLLUP وCUBE، وتنظيف النتائج بـ COALESCE وSTRING\_AGG. 8️⃣ Cheat Sheets, Exam Traps & Execution Order كل الـ Cheat Sheets وDecision Guides، أشهر 11 فخ في الامتحانات، وترتيب تنفيذ الـ SQL query. --- ## ⭐ الخلاصة النهائية (Golden Rule) ```txt OVER() ↓ Window Function PARTITION BY ↓ مين في نفس المجموعة؟ ORDER BY ↓ ما ترتيبهم؟ ROWS / RANGE ↓ أي صفوف تدخل في الحساب؟ FUNCTION ↓ ماذا أريد أن أحسب؟ ``` > قاعدة ذهبية: PARTITION BY يحدد مين مع مين، ORDER BY يحدد مين قبل مين، والـ FRAME يحدد أي صفوف تدخل الحساب. Window Functions تعمل عبر عدة صفوف مرتبطة بالـ current row، لكنها لا تختزل الصفوف مثل GROUP BY.

ORDER BY
  ↓
  ما ترتيبهم؟

ROWS / RANGE
  ↓
  أي صفوف تدخل في الحساب؟

FUNCTION
  ↓
  ماذا أريد أن أحسب؟

قاعدة ذهبية: PARTITION BY يحدد مين مع مين، ORDER BY يحدد مين قبل مين، والـ FRAME يحدد أي صفوف تدخل الحساب. Window Functions تعمل عبر عدة صفوف مرتبطة بالـ current row، لكنها لا تختزل الصفوف مثل GROUP BY.

pages.objective: Define time buckets, missing periods and independent event sequences.
pages.body: > جزء من سلسلة Intermediate SQL: هذا المرجع مخصص للتعامل مع بيانات التاريخ والوقت (Date/Time) في PostgreSQL — الأنواع، الـtimezones، الحساب الزمني، GENERATE_SERIES، وLAG/LEAD. عقلية المحلل ودليل القرار الشامل لكل المكتبة موجودين في صفحة الختام الموحّدة (مربوطة في نهاية الصفحة). # 1. الأنواع الرئيسية في PostgreSQL | النوع | بيخزن | | --- | --- | | DATE | السنة، الشهر، اليوم | | TIMESTAMP | التاريخ + الوقت | | INTERVAL | المدة بين نقطتين زمنيتين، أو كمية وقت تُضاف/تُطرح | الـTimestamps ممكن تحتوي على أجزاء من الثانية لحد الـmicroseconds. ## 1.2 ISO 8601 قيم التاريخ/الوقت في PostgreSQL بتتمثل غالبًا بصيغة واضحة تبدأ بالسنة زي: ```txt 2018-01-10 13:00:00 ``` الترتيب: ```txt year → month → day → hour → minute → second ``` المكونات الأصغر بتستخدم أصفار بادئة (leading zeros) عند الحاجة. ## 1.3 المناطق الزمنية (Time Zones) و UTC الـtimestamp ممكن يتمثل مع معلومة المنطقة الزمنية. المنطقة الزمنية بتتعبّر كـoffset من UTC، مثال: ```txt 2018-01-10 13:00:00+02 ``` لازم تفرّق بين: - timestamp بيمثل لحظة زمنية مطلقة مع سياق timezone - timestamp من غير معلومة timezone التعامل مع الـtimezone مهم جدًا للتطبيقات العالمية، سجلات الأحداث (event logs)، والتقارير عبر مناطق مختلفة. ## 1.4 مقارنة التواريخ والـTimestamps التواريخ/الـtimestamps ممكن تتقارن باستخدام: ```txt = <> < > <= >= ``` مثال: ```sql SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'; ``` الـtimestamp الحالي: ```sql SELECT NOW(); ``` ## 1.5 طرح التواريخ (Date Subtraction) طرح تاريخين/timestamps بينتج مدة (INTERVAL): ```sql SELECT end_time - start_time AS duration FROM events; ``` ده مفيد لـ: - مدة معالجة عملية - وقت انتظار العميل - الوقت بين المعاملات - وقت حل تذكرة الدعم ## 1.6 إضافة تواريخ وIntervals إضافة integer لـDATE بتضيف أيام: ```sql SELECT DATE '2026-01-10' + 7; ``` لوحدات زمنية أكبر، استخدم interval: ```sql SELECT DATE '2026-01-10' + INTERVAL '1 year'; ``` تقدر تجمع أكتر من وحدة مع بعض: ```sql SELECT TIMESTAMP '2026-01-10 10:00:00' + INTERVAL '1 year 2 days 3 minutes'; ``` > فخ: إضافة integer لـtimestamp مش زي إضافته لـdate؛ استخدم INTERVAL لأي عملية حسابية على timestamp. --- # 2. استخراج وتقريب مكونات التاريخ/الوقت ## 2.1 EXTRACT و DATE\_PART أشهر الحقول: - YEAR - MONTH - DAY - HOUR - MINUTE - SECOND - WEEK - DOW (يوم الأسبوع) - DECADE - CENTURY مثال: ```sql SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS year, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS month FROM orders; ``` نفس الفكرة بصيغة DATE_PART: ```sql SELECT DATE_PART('year', order_date) AS year, DATE_PART('month', order_date) AS month FROM orders; ``` EXTRACT وDATE_PART بيقدموا نفس العملية المفاهيمية بصياغة مختلفة. ### تذكير بخصوص DOW في PostgreSQL، DOW بتستخدم: ```txt Sunday = 0 Monday = 1 ... Saturday = 6 ``` > نصيحة: الحقول الزمنية اللي مش متعود عليها ممكن يكون لها تعريف غير متوقع. راجع توثيق PostgreSQL قبل ما تبني عليها أي business logic. ## 2.2 التجميع حسب مكوّن تاريخ مثال: قارن المبيعات شهريًا عبر عدة سنوات. ```sql SELECT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM sale_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM sales GROUP BY EXTRACT(MONTH FROM sale_date) ORDER BY month; ``` ده بيجاوب على أسئلة زي: > هل مبيعات يناير عادةً أعلى من مبيعات مارس؟ ## 2.3 DATE\_TRUNC DATE_TRUNC بتحتفظ بمستوى دقة معين وبتصفّر المكونات الأصغر. ```sql SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', TIMESTAMP '2019-07-15 14:35:22'); -- 2019-07-01 00:00:00 ``` النموذج الذهني: ```txt 2019-07-15 14:35:22 ↓ DATE_TRUNC('month') 2019-07-01 00:00:00 ``` استخدمها لما تحتاج تجمع timestamps في time buckets أكبر: ```sql SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', sale_time) AS month, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM sales GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', sale_time) ORDER BY month; ``` ### EXTRACT مقابل DATE\_TRUNC - EXTRACT(MONTH ...) → بترجع مكوّن زي 7. - DATE_TRUNC('month', ...) → بترجع timestamp يمثل بداية الشهر ده. > قاعدة القرار: لو محتاج المكوّن الرقمي نفسه، استخدم EXTRACT. لو محتاج time bucket يتم تجميعه/دمجه كـdate-like value، DATE_TRUNC غالبًا أفيد. --- # 3. GENERATE\_SERIES مع التاريخ/الوقت ## 3.1 النمط الأساسي GENERATE_SERIES تقدر تولّد بيها سلسلة من الـtimestamps. ```sql SELECT * FROM GENERATE_SERIES( '2026-01-01'::timestamp, '2026-01-05'::timestamp, INTERVAL '1 day' ) AS t(day); ``` القيم المولّدة بتستمر طالما القيمة التالية أصغر من أو تساوي قيمة النهاية. تقدر تستخدم ساعات كمان: ```sql SELECT * FROM GENERATE_SERIES( '2026-01-01 09:00'::timestamp, '2026-01-01 14:00'::timestamp, INTERVAL '1 hour' ) AS t(hour); ``` ## 3.2 ليه نولّد من بداية الفترة؟ تجنب توليد سلسلة شهرية بدءًا من يوم 31. إضافة شهر لـ31 يناير ممكن توديك لـ28 فبراير، وبعدين إضافة شهر تاني هتديك 28 مارس مش 31. النمط الآمن: ```sql SELECT month_start FROM GENERATE_SERIES( '2026-01-01'::date, '2026-12-01'::date, INTERVAL '1 month' ) AS s(month_start); ``` عشان تجيب آخر يوم في كل شهر: ```sql SELECT month_start + INTERVAL '1 month' - INTERVAL '1 day' AS month_end FROM GENERATE_SERIES( '2026-01-01'::date, '2026-12-01'::date, INTERVAL '1 month' ) AS s(month_start); ``` > قاعدة: ولّد من بدايات فترات ثابتة، واشتق نهايات الفترات بعد كده. ## 3.3 اكتشاف الفترات الزمنية المفقودة الـaggregation العادي بيرجع بس الفترات اللي فعلًا موجودة في البيانات. مثال للمشكلة: ```txt 09:00 → 5 sales 10:00 → 3 sales 12:00 → 4 sales ``` الساعة 11:00 مش ظاهرة، رغم إنها كانت فعلًا صفر مبيعات. اعمل سلسلة كاملة واعمل LEFT JOIN مع البيانات: ```sql WITH hour_series AS ( SELECT hour FROM GENERATE_SERIES( '2026-01-01 09:00'::timestamp, '2026-01-01 14:00'::timestamp, INTERVAL '1 hour' ) AS s(hour) ) SELECT h.hour, COUNT(s.sale_time) AS sales_count FROM hour_series h LEFT JOIN sales s ON DATE_TRUNC('hour', s.sale_time) = h.hour GROUP BY h.hour ORDER BY h.hour; ``` > مهم: عد عمود الحدث القابل لـNULL (COUNT(s.sale_time))، مش COUNT(*)، عشان الفترات المفقودة تبقى صفر بدل واحد. --- # 4. فترات زمنية مخصصة (Time Bins / Intervals) لما الـbucket المطلوب مش حقل تاريخ طبيعي، اعمل bins واضحة. مثال: فترات مبيعات كل 3 ساعات. ```sql WITH bins AS ( SELECT lower_bound, lower_bound + INTERVAL '3 hours' AS upper_bound FROM GENERATE_SERIES( '2026-01-01 09:00'::timestamp, '2026-01-01 15:00'::timestamp, INTERVAL '3 hours' ) AS s(lower_bound) ) SELECT b.lower_bound, b.upper_bound, COUNT(s.sale_time) AS sales_count FROM bins b LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.sale_time >= b.lower_bound AND s.sale_time < b.upper_bound GROUP BY b.lower_bound, b.upper_bound ORDER BY b.lower_bound; ``` الفترة نصف المفتوحة (half-open interval): ```txt lower_bound <= time < upper_bound ``` بتمنع القيم على الحد الفاصل من إنها تتحسب في bin-ين. --- # 5. LAG / LEAD لحساب الوقت بين الأحداث ## 5.1 المشكلة الأساسية تخيل عمود فيه كل أوقات الأحداث: ```txt 09:07 09:13 09:40 10:20 ``` السؤال: > كام وقت بيعدي بين الأحداث المتتالية؟ محتاج تجيب قيمة الصف السابق أو التالي. ## 5.2 LAG LAG(column) بترجع قيمة من صف سابق داخل window مرتبة. ```sql SELECT sale_time, LAG(sale_time) OVER ( ORDER BY sale_time ) AS previous_sale FROM sales; ``` النتيجة من الناحية المفاهيمية: | sale\_time | previous\_sale | | --- | --- | | 09:07 | NULL | | 09:13 | 09:07 | | 09:40 | 09:13 | | 10:20 | 09:40 | ## 5.3 الوقت منذ الحدث السابق ```sql SELECT sale_time, sale_time - LAG(sale_time) OVER ( ORDER BY sale_time ) AS time_since_previous FROM sales; ``` الصف الأول بيكون NULL لأنه معندوش حدث سابق. ## 5.4 LEAD LEAD(column) بترجع قيمة من الصف التالي. ```sql SELECT sale_time, LEAD(sale_time) OVER ( ORDER BY sale_time ) AS next_sale FROM sales; ``` ### مقارنة سريعة | الدالة | بتنظر لـ | سؤال نموذجي | | --- | --- | --- | | LAG() | الصف السابق | إيه اللي حصل قبل كده؟ | | LEAD() | الصف التالي | هيحصل إيه بعد كده؟ | ## 5.5 الإزاحة (Offset) الافتراضي هو 1: ```sql LAG(value) ``` صفين للخلف: ```sql LAG(value, 2) ``` صفين للقدام: ```sql LEAD(value, 2) ``` ## 5.6 متوسط الوقت بين الأحداث متعملش nest لـwindow function جوه aggregate على نفس مستوى الـquery: ```sql -- ❌ متستخدمش هذا النمط AVG(sale_time - LAG(sale_time) OVER (...)) ``` بدل من كده استخدم مرحلتين منطقيتين: ```sql SELECT AVG(time_between) FROM ( SELECT sale_time - LAG(sale_time) OVER ( ORDER BY sale_time ) AS time_between FROM sales ) AS gaps; ``` النموذج الذهني: ```txt Events ↓ LAG() ↓ Time between events ↓ Subquery / CTE ↓ AVG() ``` ## 5.7 LAG لتغيّر السلسلة الزمنية LAG/LEAD مش مقتصرة على الـtimestamps. مثال: ```sql SELECT sale_date, sales, sales - LAG(sales) OVER ( ORDER BY sale_date ) AS change_from_previous FROM daily_sales; ``` ده بيدّيك: ```txt current value - previous value ``` لحساب النسبة المئوية للتغيّر: ```txt (current - previous) / previous × 100 ``` التطبيق القوي غالبًا بيحسب القيمة السابقة مرة واحدة في CTE/subquery وبعدين يستخدمها في الخطوة اللي بعدها. ## 5.8 PARTITION BY مع LAG/LEAD لو فيه كيانات مستقلة متعددة، اعمل partition للـwindow. مثال: الوقت بين الأحداث لكل عميل: ```sql SELECT customer_id, event_time, LAG(event_time) OVER ( PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY event_time ) AS previous_event FROM customer_events; ``` النموذج الذهني: ```txt PARTITION BY → مين مع مين؟ ORDER BY → مين قبل مين؟ LAG/LEAD → أجيب قيمة منين؟ ``` من غير PARTITION BY، ممكن يتقارن حدث عميل بحدث عميل تاني بالغلط. > لمرجع أشمل عن Window Functions يغطي الـranking، الـframes، FIRST_VALUE، LAST_VALUE، ROLLUP، CUBE، وأكتر، راجع مرجع SQL Window Functions — Complete Reference Guide المربوط بالفعل في هذه المكتبة. --- # 6. حالات استخدام واقعية (Real-World Use Cases) ## حالة الاستخدام 1 — SLA لدعم العملاء الهدف: > كل تذكرة دعم بتاخد قد إيه لحد ما تتحل؟ ```sql SELECT ticket_id, created_at, resolved_at, resolved_at - created_at AS resolution_time FROM tickets; ``` وبعدين اعمل aggregate: ```sql SELECT AVG(resolution_time) FROM ( SELECT resolved_at - created_at AS resolution_time FROM tickets ) t; ``` استخدام في الشغل: - مراقبة SLA - تخطيط الموارد البشرية (Staffing) - اكتشاف الطوابير البطيئة - مقارنة الفرق/التصنيفات ## حالة الاستخدام 2 — فجوات مبيعات التجارة الإلكترونية الهدف: > إيه متوسط الوقت بين طلبات نفس العميل؟ ```sql SELECT AVG(time_between) FROM ( SELECT customer_id, order_time - LAG(order_time) OVER ( PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_time ) AS time_between FROM orders ) t; ``` استخدام في الشغل: - تكرار الشراء - سلوك إعادة الطلب - تفاعل العميل - إشارات الـchurn ## حالة الاستخدام 3 — اتجاه المبيعات الشهري ```sql WITH monthly_sales AS ( SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', sale_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM sales GROUP BY 1 ) SELECT month, revenue, revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER ( ORDER BY month ) AS mom_change FROM monthly_sales ORDER BY month; ``` ده نمط تحليل Month-over-Month (MoM) كلاسيكي. ## حالة الاستخدام 4 — مراقبة اكتمال البيانات الهدف: > أي ساعات/أيام كانت بصفر أحداث؟ اعمل سلسلة زمنية كاملة باستخدام GENERATE_SERIES، وبعدين LEFT JOIN مع بيانات الـfact. ده مفيد جدًا لـ: - مراقبة ETL - IoT/event streams - زيارات الموقع - أنظمة المعاملات - التقارير التشغيلية --- # 7. الخاتمة ودليل القرار الشامل عقلية المحلل، والـcheat sheet الكامل، والقواعد الذهبية النهائية اتنقلوا لصفحة واحدة موحّدة تخص المكتبة كلها (مش موديول Text/Date-Time بس)، عشان محتوى الختام كان مكرر حرفيًا بين الصفحتين: --- > قواعد سريعة خاصة بالتاريخ/الوقت (مقتطف من الخاتمة الشاملة): استخدم EXTRACT للمكوّن الرقمي، وDATE_TRUNC للـtime buckets؛ استخدم GENERATE_SERIES لما الفترات المفقودة نفسها تكون مهمة تحليليًا؛ استخدم LAG/LEAD للمقارنات بين صف وصف؛ واستخدم PARTITION BY لما التسلسل لازم يكون مستقل لكل كيان. القواعد الذهبية الكاملة والـcheat sheet الشامل لكل المكتبة في صفحة الختام المربوطة فوق.

blocks.text: الـTimestamps ممكن تحتوي على أجزاء من الثانية لحد الـmicroseconds.
قيم التاريخ/الوقت في PostgreSQL بتتمثل غالبًا بصيغة واضحة تبدأ بالسنة زي:
year → month → day → hour → minute → second
المكونات الأصغر بتستخدم أصفار بادئة (leading zeros) عند الحاجة.
الـtimestamp ممكن يتمثل مع معلومة المنطقة الزمنية. المنطقة الزمنية بتتعبّر كـoffset من UTC، مثال:

items: timestamp بيمثل لحظة زمنية مطلقة مع سياق timezone

blocks.text: التعامل مع الـtimezone مهم جدًا للتطبيقات العالمية، سجلات الأحداث (event logs)، والتقارير عبر مناطق مختلفة.

SELECT end_time - start_time AS duration
FROM events;
تقدر تجمع أكتر من وحدة مع بعض:

SELECT TIMESTAMP '2026-01-10 10:00:00'
       + INTERVAL '1 year 2 days 3 minutes';
فخ: إضافة integer لـtimestamp مش زي إضافته لـdate؛ استخدم INTERVAL لأي عملية حسابية على timestamp.

SELECT
    EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS year,
    EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS month
FROM orders;

SELECT
    DATE_PART('year', order_date) AS year,
    DATE_PART('month', order_date) AS month
FROM orders;
EXTRACT وDATE_PART بيقدموا نفس العملية المفاهيمية بصياغة مختلفة.
نصيحة: الحقول الزمنية اللي مش متعود عليها ممكن يكون لها تعريف غير متوقع. راجع توثيق PostgreSQL قبل ما تبني عليها أي business logic.
مثال: قارن المبيعات شهريًا عبر عدة سنوات.

SELECT
    EXTRACT(MONTH FROM sale_date) AS month,
    SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM sales
GROUP BY EXTRACT(MONTH FROM sale_date)
ORDER BY month;
هل مبيعات يناير عادةً أعلى من مبيعات مارس؟
DATE_TRUNC بتحتفظ بمستوى دقة معين وبتصفّر المكونات الأصغر.
استخدمها لما تحتاج تجمع timestamps في time buckets أكبر:

SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', sale_time) AS month,
    SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM sales
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', sale_time)
ORDER BY month;

items: DATE_TRUNC('month', ...) → بترجع timestamp يمثل بداية الشهر ده.

blocks.text: قاعدة القرار: لو محتاج المكوّن الرقمي نفسه، استخدم EXTRACT. لو محتاج time bucket يتم تجميعه/دمجه كـdate-like value، DATE_TRUNC غالبًا أفيد.
GENERATE_SERIES تقدر تولّد بيها سلسلة من الـtimestamps.
القيم المولّدة بتستمر طالما القيمة التالية أصغر من أو تساوي قيمة النهاية.
تجنب توليد سلسلة شهرية بدءًا من يوم 31. إضافة شهر لـ31 يناير ممكن توديك لـ28 فبراير، وبعدين إضافة شهر تاني هتديك 28 مارس مش 31.
عشان تجيب آخر يوم في كل شهر:
قاعدة: ولّد من بدايات فترات ثابتة، واشتق نهايات الفترات بعد كده.
الـaggregation العادي بيرجع بس الفترات اللي فعلًا موجودة في البيانات.
الساعة 11:00 مش ظاهرة، رغم إنها كانت فعلًا صفر مبيعات.
اعمل سلسلة كاملة واعمل LEFT JOIN مع البيانات:

WITH hour_series AS (
    SELECT hour
    FROM GENERATE_SERIES(
        '2026-01-01 09:00'::timestamp,
        '2026-01-01 14:00'::timestamp,
        INTERVAL '1 hour'
    ) AS s(hour)
)
SELECT
    h.hour,
    COUNT(s.sale_time) AS sales_count
FROM hour_series h
LEFT JOIN sales s
    ON DATE_TRUNC('hour', s.sale_time) = h.hour
GROUP BY h.hour
ORDER BY h.hour;
مهم: عد عمود الحدث القابل لـNULL (COUNT(s.sale_time))، مش COUNT(*)، عشان الفترات المفقودة تبقى صفر بدل واحد.
لما الـbucket المطلوب مش حقل تاريخ طبيعي، اعمل bins واضحة.

WITH bins AS (
    SELECT
        lower_bound,
        lower_bound + INTERVAL '3 hours' AS upper_bound
    FROM GENERATE_SERIES(
        '2026-01-01 09:00'::timestamp,
        '2026-01-01 15:00'::timestamp,
        INTERVAL '3 hours'
    ) AS s(lower_bound)
)
SELECT
    b.lower_bound,
    b.upper_bound,
    COUNT(s.sale_time) AS sales_count
FROM bins b
LEFT JOIN sales s
    ON s.sale_time >= b.lower_bound
   AND s.sale_time < b.upper_bound
GROUP BY b.lower_bound, b.upper_bound
ORDER BY b.lower_bound;
بتمنع القيم على الحد الفاصل من إنها تتحسب في bin-ين.
5. LAG / LEAD لحساب الوقت بين الأحداث
تخيل عمود فيه كل أوقات الأحداث:
كام وقت بيعدي بين الأحداث المتتالية؟
محتاج تجيب قيمة الصف السابق أو التالي.
LAG(column) بترجع قيمة من صف سابق داخل window مرتبة.
الصف الأول بيكون NULL لأنه معندوش حدث سابق.
متعملش nest لـwindow function جوه aggregate على نفس مستوى الـquery:

-- ❌ متستخدمش هذا النمط
AVG(sale_time - LAG(sale_time) OVER (...))
بدل من كده استخدم مرحلتين منطقيتين:

Events
  ↓
LAG()
  ↓
Time between events
  ↓
Subquery / CTE
  ↓
AVG()

SELECT
    sale_date,
    sales,
    sales - LAG(sales) OVER (
        ORDER BY sale_date
    ) AS change_from_previous
FROM daily_sales;
التطبيق القوي غالبًا بيحسب القيمة السابقة مرة واحدة في CTE/subquery وبعدين يستخدمها في الخطوة اللي بعدها.
لو فيه كيانات مستقلة متعددة، اعمل partition للـwindow.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    event_time,
    LAG(event_time) OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer_id
        ORDER BY event_time
    ) AS previous_event
FROM customer_events;

PARTITION BY → مين مع مين؟
ORDER BY     → مين قبل مين؟
LAG/LEAD     → أجيب قيمة منين؟
من غير PARTITION BY، ممكن يتقارن حدث عميل بحدث عميل تاني بالغلط.
لمرجع أشمل عن Window Functions يغطي الـranking، الـframes، FIRST_VALUE، LAST_VALUE، ROLLUP، CUBE، وأكتر، راجع مرجع SQL Window Functions — Complete Reference Guide المربوط بالفعل في هذه المكتبة.
كل تذكرة دعم بتاخد قد إيه لحد ما تتحل؟

SELECT
    ticket_id,
    created_at,
    resolved_at,
    resolved_at - created_at AS resolution_time
FROM tickets;
حالة الاستخدام 2 — فجوات مبيعات التجارة الإلكترونية
إيه متوسط الوقت بين طلبات نفس العميل؟

WITH monthly_sales AS (
    SELECT
        DATE_TRUNC('month', sale_date) AS month,
        SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM sales
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    month,
    revenue,
    revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (
        ORDER BY month
    ) AS mom_change
FROM monthly_sales
ORDER BY month;
اعمل سلسلة زمنية كاملة باستخدام GENERATE_SERIES، وبعدين LEFT JOIN مع بيانات الـfact. ده مفيد جدًا لـ:
عقلية المحلل، والـcheat sheet الكامل، والقواعد الذهبية النهائية اتنقلوا لصفحة واحدة موحّدة تخص المكتبة كلها (مش موديول Text/Date-Time بس)، عشان محتوى الختام كان مكرر حرفيًا بين الصفحتين:

قواعد سريعة خاصة بالتاريخ/الوقت (مقتطف من الخاتمة الشاملة): استخدم EXTRACT للمكوّن الرقمي، وDATE_TRUNC للـtime buckets؛ استخدم GENERATE_SERIES لما الفترات المفقودة نفسها تكون مهمة تحليليًا؛ استخدم LAG/LEAD للمقارنات بين صف وصف؛ واستخدم PARTITION BY لما التسلسل لازم يكون مستقل لكل كيان. القواعد الذهبية الكاملة والـcheat sheet الشامل لكل المكتبة في صفحة الختام المربوطة فوق.

pages.objective: Clean and classify text without confusing NULL, empty strings and spaces.
pages.body: > جزء من سلسلة Intermediate SQL: هذا المرجع مخصص للتعامل مع البيانات النصية (Character / Text Data) في PostgreSQL — الأنواع، تنظيف البيانات، الـpattern matching، التقسيم، والدمج. ## 1.1 أنواع البيانات النصية في PostgreSQL عندك ثلاثة أنواع رئيسية: | النوع | المعنى | نقطة مهمة | | --- | --- | --- | | CHAR(n) | نص بطول ثابت (Fixed-length) | القيم الأقصر بيتم padding لها بمسافات؛ المسافات الزايدة في النهاية بتتجاهل عند المقارنة. | | VARCHAR(n) | نص متغير الطول بحد أقصى اختياري | يخزن قيم لحد الطول الأقصى المحدد. | | TEXT | نص متغير الطول | من غير حد أقصى معلن. | > مهم: نوع الـdatabase والدور التحليلي للنص مفهومان مختلفان. عمود TEXT ممكن يحتوي على بيانات categorical أو نص غير منظم (unstructured). ## 1.2 نص تصنيفي (Categorical) مقابل نص غير منظم (Unstructured) ### النص التصنيفي (Categorical) قيم قصيرة ومتكررة من مجموعة محدودة وقابلة للإدارة. أمثلة: - Product category - Day of week - Gender/status fields حيث يُسمح - إجابات Multiple-choice في الاستبيانات أول تحليل نموذجي: ```sql SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY n DESC; ``` ### النص غير المنظم (Unstructured) نصوص أطول وغالبًا فريدة مثل: - مراجعات المنتجات (Product reviews) - إجابات الاستبيانات المفتوحة - تعليقات العملاء - تذاكر الدعم الفني للنص غير المنظم، التحليل غالبًا بيعني استخراج features زي: - وجود keyword معين - طول النص - مؤشرات مرتبطة بالـsentiment - الموضوع/التصنيف - Binary flags زي contains_refund_keyword ## 1.3 أول EDA للنص التصنيفي افحص دايمًا القيم المميزة (distinct values) والتكرار (frequency) مع بعض. ```sql SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY n DESC; ``` وبعدين افحص أبجديًا: ```sql SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category; ``` ### ليه الاتنين؟ - ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC → بيكشف التصنيفات الشائعة/النادرة. - ORDER BY category → بيسهّل اكتشاف اختلافات الحالة (case)، المسافات، والقيم اللي شكلها مكرر. ## 1.4 مشاكل شائعة في البيانات النصية انتبه لـ: - اختلاف حالة الأحرف: Apple, apple, APPLE - مسافات في البداية/النهاية: ' apple', 'apple ' - تباعد داخلي مختلف - string فارغ: '' - قيمة مكونة من مسافات فقط: ' ' - NULL - اختلافات في علامات الترقيم، وحتى الشرطات المتشابهة بصريًا - اختلاف مفرد/جمع: apple مقابل apples > تمييز حرج: NULL، والـstring الفارغ، والـstring اللي فيه مسافات بس — ثلاث قيم مختلفة تمامًا. ## 1.5 تحويل حالة الأحرف (Case Conversion) ```sql LOWER(column) UPPER(column) ``` مثال: ```sql SELECT LOWER(fav_fruit) AS fruit_lower FROM survey; ``` الدوال دي بتغيّر حالة الأحرف بس، ومش بتغيّر الأرقام أو علامات الترقيم. ### نمط المقارنة بدون حساسية لحالة الأحرف ```sql SELECT * FROM survey WHERE LOWER(fav_fruit) = 'apple'; ``` ده بيحل مشكلة اختلاف الحالة بس مش المسافات الزايدة أو صيغة الجمع. ## 1.6 LIKE مقابل ILIKE LIKE بتعمل pattern matching. - % = أي عدد من الأحرف، حتى صفر. - _ = حرف واحد بالظبط. مثال: ```sql SELECT * FROM survey WHERE fav_fruit LIKE '%apple%'; ``` ده ممكن يطابق أي قيمة فيها apple في أي مكان من الـstring. ILIKE بتعمل pattern match بدون حساسية لحالة الأحرف في PostgreSQL: ```sql SELECT * FROM survey WHERE fav_fruit ILIKE '%apple%'; ``` > ملاحظة أداء: ILIKE ممكن تكون أبطأ من LIKE؛ استخدمها بس لما فعلًا تحتاج مطابقة case-insensitive. ### ⚠️ فخ LIKE LIKE '%apple%' بتطابق كمان pineapple. لو محتاج قيمة مطابقة تمامًا بعد التطبيع، الأفضل: ```sql WHERE LOWER(TRIM(fav_fruit)) = 'apple' ``` ## 1.7 إزالة المسافات (Trimming) ```sql TRIM(column) -- من الطرفين BTRIM(column) -- من الطرفين LTRIM(column) -- من اليسار/البداية RTRIM(column) -- من اليمين/النهاية ``` افتراضيًا دول بيشيلوا الـspace العادي بس، مش كل أنواع الـwhitespace زي الـtabs/newlines. تقدر كمان تحدد أحرف معينة تتشال: ```sql TRIM(BOTH '!' FROM column) ``` قائمة الأحرف دي case-sensitive، يعني w وW أحرف مختلفة. ## 1.8 دمج الدوال مع بعض الدوال ممكن تتعشش (nested). الدالة الداخلية بتتنفذ الأول. ```sql TRIM(LOWER(fav_fruit)) ``` النموذج الذهني: ```txt fav_fruit ↓ LOWER() ↓ TRIM() ↓ standardized value ``` نمط تطبيع شائع: ```sql LOWER(TRIM(column)) ``` ## 1.9 تقسيم واستخراج النص > مرجع الـ LEFT/RIGHT/SUBSTRING بالتفصيل (مع real use cases، FROM/FOR syntax، ومثال متقدم لتجميع الدوال — nested functions لتحليل إيميل) موجود في [4️⃣ String & Character Functions](https://app.notion.com/p/3cb3906c5d6c81f981e3cff58e8ce989) جوه PostgreSQL Data Manipulation — منتكررشش هنا. والصفحة دي برضو بتغطي LENGTH/CHAR_LENGTH وPOSITION/STRPOS اللي مش موجودة هنا خالص. ### إشارة سريعة ```sql LEFT(column, n) RIGHT(column, n) SUBSTRING(column FROM start FOR length) ``` ## 1.10 التقسيم عند فاصل معين (Delimiter) SPLIT_PART(string, delimiter, position) بترجع جزء واحد بعد التقسيم عند delimiter معين. ```sql SELECT SPLIT_PART('a,bc,d', ',', 2); -- bc ``` الـdelimiter ممكن يكون حرف واحد أو أكتر: ```sql SELECT SPLIT_PART('cats and dogs and fish', ' and ', 2); -- dogs ``` > الـdelimiter بيتطابق بالظبط زي ما هو مكتوب، مش كمجموعة أحرف منفصلة. ## 1.11 الدمج (Concatenation) باستخدام CONCAT: ```sql SELECT CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name FROM customers; ``` باستخدام عملية الدمج ||: ```sql SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name FROM customers; ``` ### فرق مهم بخصوص NULL - CONCAT() بتتجاهل الـNULL arguments. - || بترجع NULL لو أي جزء كان NULL. الفرق ده مهم لما تبني أسماء، أو labels، أو عناوين، أو identifiers. ## 1.12 تحويلات متعددة: CASE WHEN لما صفوف مختلفة تحتاج تحويلات مختلفة والحالات مش متداخلة، استخدم CASE. مثال: تصنيف بيستخدم delimiters مختلفة (: , | , - ): ```sql SELECT CASE WHEN category LIKE '%: %' THEN SPLIT_PART(category, ': ', 1) WHEN category LIKE '% | %' THEN SPLIT_PART(category, ' | ', 1) ELSE SPLIT_PART(category, ' - ', 1) END AS major_category FROM industries; ``` > النمط: حدد صيغة الـrow الأول، وبعدين طبّق التحويل المناسب لتلك الصيغة. ## 1.13 نمط جدول إعادة الترميز (Recoding Table) لما يكون فيه قيم فوضوية كتير أو محتاج mappings صريحة، جدول مؤقت لإعادة الترميز غالبًا بيكون أوضح من CASE ضخمة. ### الخطوة 1 — إنشاء جدول الـmapping ```sql CREATE TEMP TABLE fruit_recode AS SELECT DISTINCT fav_fruit AS original, fav_fruit AS standardized FROM survey; ``` ### الخطوة 2 — تحديث القيم الموحّدة ```sql UPDATE fruit_recode SET standardized = LOWER(TRIM(original)); ``` تصحيحات إضافية مستهدفة ممكن تستخدم WHERE: ```sql UPDATE fruit_recode SET standardized = 'banana' WHERE original LIKE '%nn%'; ``` ### الخطوة 3 — ربط الـmapping بالبيانات الأصلية ```sql SELECT r.standardized, COUNT(*) AS n FROM survey s JOIN fruit_recode r ON s.fav_fruit = r.original GROUP BY r.standardized ORDER BY n DESC; ``` > متى تفضّل أسلوب جدول الـmapping: استثناءات صريحة كتير، mappings قابلة لإعادة الاستخدام، منطق تنظيف قابل للتدقيق (auditable)، أو محتاج تفصل القيم الخام عن القيم الموحّدة.
